en: The *Śuka-sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
[In] the garden.
At that time, the Blessed One rose early in the morning, put on his robes, and together with his bowl, went to Śrāvastī for alms.
While wandering through Śrāvastī for alms, he arrived at the house of the parrot-keeper Māṭhara.
At that time, Śuka Māṭhara was away on some business.
At that time, Śuka Māṭhara had a dog named Guḍa, who sat upon a fine cushion and ate polished rice and meat from a golden bowl.
The white dog saw the World-Honored One approaching from afar, and upon seeing him, it barked.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these words: "Cease!"
“White dog!
You need not make such a sound; you were originally the chanting voice of a brahmin begging for alms!
Thereupon, the white dog became extremely angry and displeased; having descended from its bedding, it went to the threshold of the door and lay down there, remaining silent and still.

Later, after Mālakīmāta had returned to his house, he saw that the white dog had descended from its bed and was lying silently by the door-sill, dejected and unhappy. Having seen this, he asked those around him:
"Who has provoked or troubled this white dog, such that it is dejected and unhappy, having descended from its bed and now lying silently by the door-sill?"
“Māluṅkyāputra! There is no one who has provoked or disturbed this dog, yet it is distressed and unhappy; having descended from its bed and bedding, it lies prostrate and silent by the threshold.”
"O Māluṅkyaputta!
Today the śramaṇa Gautama came to our home to beg for alms, and that white dog barked at him. That śramaṇa Gautama then said this:
'Stop!'"
"White dog!
You should not make such a sound; you were originally meant for chanting!
For this reason, Māluṅkyaputta!
He caused the white dog to become angry and displeased, and having descended from his bed and mat, he lay prostrate in silence upon the threshold.

Thereupon, Śuka Māṭhara the Tauriya became angry and displeased with the Blessed One; he reviled the Blessed One from afar, slandered the Blessed One from afar, and bore malice toward the Blessed One from afar, saying:
"This ascetic Gautama!..."
"to speak such false and delusive words!
Having departed from Śrāvastī, he went to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of people as he preached the Dharma.
The Blessed One saw from afar the parrot Māluṅkyaputra approaching, and having seen him, he addressed the bhikṣus: "O bhikṣus!..."
"Do you see Śuka Māṭhara the Tauriya coming from afar?
"Indeed, World-Honored One.
"If Śuka Māṭhara the Tauriya were to pass away at this very moment, he would be reborn in hell in the time it takes to extend or contract one's arm."
Why is this? Because he was thus extremely angry toward me; due to that anger, at the dissolution of the body after death, he was reborn in an evil destination, in the hells.
At that time, Śuka Māṭhara came to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"O Śramaṇa Gautama!
"Have you come to my house today to beg for alms?
He replied,
"Māluṅkyaputta!"
"I have come to your house today to beg for alms.
"Indeed, O Śramaṇa Gautama!
What offense has that white dog committed against you, such that it causes my white dog to become angry and displeased, to descend from its bed and mat, and to lie down silently by the door-sill?"
He replied: "Māluṅkyaputta!
Having risen early this morning and put on my robes, I took my bowl and went to Śrāvastī for alms. While wandering through Śrāvastī for alms, I arrived at your house."
"Your white dog saw me coming from afar; having seen me, it barked, and I spoke these words:
'Stop, white dog!'"
"You should not make such a sound; you were originally meant for chanting!
For this reason, Māluṅkyaputta, that white dog became angry and displeased, descended from the bed and bedding, and lay down silently by the threshold of the door.
“Gautama, who was this white dog originally related to as a kinsman? “Stop!”
“Māluṅkyaputra!
There is no need to ask; you might become distressed and unhappy upon hearing it.
A second and a third time, the parrot Māluṅkyaputra addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"O Gautama! What kind of relative was this white dog originally?
"Māluṅkyaputta! [the Buddha replied.]
"Since you have asked me this repeatedly, I shall explain it to you.
Māluṅkyaputra!
That white dog born previously was your father; his name was Tūla."

Thereupon, Śuka Māṭhara, his anger toward the Blessed One increasing all the more and being dissatisfied, reviled the Blessed One, was incensed with the Blessed One, and slandered the Blessed One, saying:
"This śramaṇa Gautama!..."
"False speech!
He addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"O Gautama! This..."

"My father Dora constantly practiced giving, constantly offered the gift of banners, and constantly served the sacrificial fire; after his body perished and he died, he was reborn in the sublime Brahma Heaven. For what reason, then, would he be reborn among dogs?"
“Māluṅkyaputra! Because of your overweening pride, your father Dora was likewise; for this reason, you were born among the base and wicked dogs.
He then spoke a verse:
“The brahmin of overweening pride, at the end of this life, will be born in the six realms:
as a rooster, a pig, a dog, a wild fox, a donkey, or an egg-born being in hell.
“You, Māluṅkyaputta!”
"Māṭhara, if you do not believe what I have said, you may now return home.
Once you arrive, speak thus to the white dog: [insert the rest of the instruction]."
"Truly, white dog!
If you were my father Dōla in your previous birth, then go back up onto the bed and bedding.
Thus, Māluṅkyaputta!
That white dog then returned to the bed and bedding and said, "O white dog!
When you were born in your previous life as my father Dōra, you used to eat polished rice and meat from a golden bowl."
"O Māluṅkyaputta!
That white dog shall eat rice and meat from a golden bowl.
O white dog!"
‘When I was born, he was my father Dhoṇa; he should show me my father’s inherited wealth, which you originally stored away and I do not know where it is.
Thus, Māḷaṅka!
"That white dog shall show you the paternal inheritance left by your father, which you do not yet know.
Thereupon, Śuka Māṭhara the Tauriya, having heard what the Blessed One had said, reflected upon it well, memorized it, and after circumambulating the Blessed One, departed from him and returned home.
Having arrived, he spoke thus to the white dog: "O white dog!
If you were my father Dora in a previous birth, you should return and sit upon the bed and bedding."
The white dog then returned and sat upon the bed and bedding. "O white dog!
If you were my father Dora in a previous life, you should eat rice and meat from this golden bowl."
That white dog then ate the rice and meat from the golden bowl.
[The householder said: "O white dog!
If you were my father Dora in a previous birth, you should show me the inheritance left by my father; you hid it away in the past, and I do not know its location now."

Thereupon, that white dog descended from the bed and went to its original resting place; having arrived, it scratched at the ground beneath all four legs of the bed with its mouth and paws, causing the parrot Māṭhara to obtain a great deal of wealth.

Thereupon, Śuka Māṭhara the son of Dōla obtained great wealth and gained immense profit; filled with extreme joy and inspired by a virtuous mind, he knelt on his right knee, joined his palms toward the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍika, and three times proclaimed his own name and lineage: "The Truly Realized Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"Truly, Śramaṇa Gautama!
You do not speak falsely, Śramaṇa Gautama!
Having thus declared his own name and lineage three times, he departed from the city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds who were listening to his teaching of the Dharma.
Seeing from afar the parrot Māluṅkyaputra approaching, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "O bhikṣus!..."
"Do you see that parrot, Mālakandika-putra, coming from afar?
"Indeed, World-Honored One.
"If the parrot Mālakandika-putra were to pass away at this very moment, he would be reborn in a happy realm in the time it takes to bend or stretch one's arm."
"Why is that? Because they have a virtuous mind toward me; by virtue of that virtuous mind, when their bodies perish at death, these beings will be reborn in a good destination, in the heavens.
At that time, the parrot Māluṅkyaputta went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings, he withdrew and sat to one side.
Once the parrot Māluṅkyaputta had sat down to one side, the Blessed One said to him:
"Māluṅkyaputta!
Is it not exactly as I have described, that the white dog is just as I have spoken?"
“Just as the śramaṇa Gautama has said, the white dog is indeed exactly as you have described, without any difference. Śramaṇa Gautama!
I wish to ask you something further; please listen to my question.”
“Māluṅkyāputta! Ask whatever you wish.
“Gautama! [he replied.]
By what cause and by what condition do those who are all born with human bodies nonetheless experience differences of high and low, good and bad, pure and turbid?

O Gautama! Why is it that among them there are those with long lives and those with short lives; those free from illness and those afflicted by illness; those who are handsome and those who are ugly; those who are noble and those who are base; those who are capable and those who are incapable; those with great wealth and those without much wealth; and those with poor wisdom and those with wisdom?
“Māluṅkyaputta!

It is because of beings, because of their conduct, because of the conditions of their conduct, and because of the actions they perform, that according to the conduct performed by those beings, various things become good or evil, high or low.”
“O Śramaṇa Gautama! What you have briefly stated has not yet been explained in detail; I do not understand its meaning.
I only pray that the Śramaṇa Gautama will explain it well for me, so that I may follow it.”
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
Regarding the Dharma you have briefly taught, which has not yet been extensively analyzed, its meaning should be understood.
"Therefore, Māluṅkyāputra!"
"Listen well and reflect upon it carefully; I shall speak for you.
"So be it, Gautama! the parrot Māluṅkyāputta replied, accepting the instruction of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Māluṅkyāputta!
What is the cause, what is the condition, by which some men or women have short lifespans?"
"O Māluṅkyaputta!

Suppose there is a man or a woman who excessively soils their hands with blood, who is near to evil and devoid of compassion, and who takes the lives of all living beings down to the smallest ant. Because of this conduct, through such causes and such actions, when the body breaks up at death, they are reborn in an evil destination, in hell; and when they come back to birth in this human world, their life is short."
Why is that? Māluṅkyaputta!
Because their conduct is deficient, some men or women commit the taking of life; this is why it is so, Māluṅkyaputta!
Because one sees that this is the result of such conduct.
Furthermore, Māluṅkyāputra, what is the cause and what is the condition by which some man or woman possesses a long life?
"O Māluṅkyaputta!

Suppose there is a man or a woman who abandons killing and leaves it behind, laying aside the sword and staff, always possessing a sense of shame, wishing for the well-being of all living beings, and purifying their intent toward killing. Because of this practice, through such causes and such conduct, when the body breaks up at death, they go to a good destination, the heavenly realms; and when they return to this human world, their life span is long."
Why is that? Māluṅkyaputta!
Because for the sake of a long life, he causes a certain man or woman to abstain from killing and abandon killing; this, Māluṅkyaputta, is [the reason].
One should know this as the retribution for such conduct. Māluṅkyaputta!
What is the cause, what is the condition, that causes a certain man or woman to have much illness?
Māluṅkyāputta!

Suppose a man or a woman harms living beings—whether by hand, by stone, by staff, or by sword—and because of that conduct, through such causes and such actions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a state of misery, in hell; and when they come back to this human world, they are subject to much illness and pain.
Why is that? Māluṅkyāputra!
Because he practices such conduct that causes illness, he brings affliction upon various beings, whether men or women; for this reason, Māluṅkyāputra!
One should know this is due to the retribution of such conduct.
Furthermore, Māluṅkyāputra! What cause and what condition lead to a certain man or woman being free from illness?

Māluṅkyaputta, suppose there is a man or a woman who does not harm living beings; because they do not harm living beings—neither with their hands, nor with stones, nor with swords, nor with clubs—they, by virtue of this conduct, for this reason, and on account of this conduct, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly worlds, and when returning to the human realm, they are free from illness and pain.
Why is this so? Māluṅkyāputra!
Because he practices the conduct of being free from illness, he causes certain men or women not to harm or disturb living beings; for this reason, Māluṅkyāputra!
One should know this as the result of such conduct.
Furthermore, Mālakīmāta! What is the cause, what is the condition, by which some men or women are ugly?

"O Māluṅkyaputta! Suppose there is a man or a woman who is full of anger and full of sorrow. When they say even a little, they become angry, sorrowful, and unhappy; dwelling in anger and giving rise to anger, they engage in extensive slander. Because of this conduct, because of this cause, and because of this behavior, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in an evil destination, in hell; and when they return to birth as humans, their physical form is wretched and ugly."
Why is this? Because he has committed evil deeds, causing some man or woman to become angry, sorrowful, and distressed;
for this reason, Māluṅkyāputra, you should know that this is the retribution for such conduct.
"Furthermore, Māluṅkyaputta!
What is the cause, what is the condition, by which some man or woman possesses a beautiful form?
Māluṅkyaputta!"

Suppose there is a man or a woman who is not prone to much anger or much sorrowful distress. If someone speaks to them with harsh and rude words, they do not become angry, nor resentful, nor distressed; they do not dwell in anger, they do not give rise to hatred, and they do not harbor resentment. Because of this conduct, by means of this conduct, and for the sake of this conduct, when their body breaks up at death, they are reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly realms; and when they return to this human world, their physical form and appearance are exquisite.
Why is this so? Māluṅkyaputta!
Because he practices sublime conduct, he causes certain men or women to be free from ill will and free from sorrow; for this reason, Māluṅkyaputta!
It should be known that this is due to the retribution of past actions.
Furthermore, Māluṅkyāputra, what is the cause and what is the condition by which a certain man or woman possesses some degree of capability?
"O Māluṅkyaputta!

Suppose there is a man or a woman who possesses covetousness and gives rise to covetousness; seeing another person respectfully bestowing wealth and goods, they give rise to covetousness, thinking, 'May I obtain what belongs to that other. Because of this conduct, because of that conduct, and conditioned by that conduct, when their body breaks up at death, they are reborn in an evil destination, in hell; and when they return to birth in this human world, they possess little capability."
For what reason?
Māluṅkyāputra!
Because he performs only a small amount of capable conduct, it causes some man or woman to give rise to greed and envy out of their own greed and envy. This, Māluṅkyāputra!
One should know this is due to the retribution of such conduct.
Furthermore, Māluṅkyāputra! For what cause and for what condition does a certain man or woman become exceedingly capable?
"O Māluṅkyaputta!

Suppose there is a man or a woman who is without covetousness and does not give rise to covetousness; seeing others being honored and given gifts of wealth, they do not give rise to covetousness, thinking, 'May what belongs to others be obtained by me. By this conduct, because of this conduct and conditioned by this conduct, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world; and when they return to birth as a human, they will be extremely capable."
Why is that? Māluṅkyāputta!
Because he has performed deeds of supreme capability, he causes certain men or women to be free from greed and envy, and not to give rise to greed and envy.
Therefore, Māluṅkyaputta!
You should know this as the result of such conduct.
This, Māluṅkyaputta!
Furthermore, by what cause and by what condition is it that some man or woman is born into a low-born family? Māluṅkyaputta! It is because some man or woman is haughty and arrogant;

they do not show respect where respect is due, do not serve where service is due, do not honor where honor is due, do not make offerings where offerings are due, do not offer seats where a seat should be offered, and do not provide guidance where guidance should be provided; nor do they honor, rise to greet with reverence, and join their palms in salutation toward those who deserve such treatment. By reason of these actions, conditioned by these actions, and because of these actions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in an evil destination, in hell, and when returning to the human world, they are born into a low-born family.
For what reason?
Māluṅkyāputra!
Because of such base conduct, some men or women become conceited and arrogant.
This is it, Māluṅkyāputra!
You should know this because of the retribution for such conduct.
This, Māluṅkyāputra!

Furthermore, what is the cause and what is the condition that causes a certain man or woman to be born into a noble and wealthy family? Māluṅkyaputta! Suppose there is a certain man or woman who is not arrogant and not conceited;

they respect those who deserve to be respected, serve those who deserve to be served, honor those who deserve to be honored, make offerings to those who deserve to be offered to, provide seats for those who deserve to be provided with seats, and guide those who deserve to be guided. They honor them, rise to show respect, and join their palms toward them. Because of this conduct, because of this condition, and by virtue of this conduct, when their body breaks up at death, they are reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly worlds; and having come back to this human world, they are born into a noble and wealthy family.
For what reason? Mālakīmāta!
Because he has practiced the conduct of the noble and distinguished, he causes certain men or women to be neither conceited nor arrogant.
This, Māluṅkyāputta,
you should know as the result of such conduct.
This, Māluṅkyāputta!
Furthermore, what is the cause and what is the condition by which some man or woman possesses little wealth?
Māluṅkyāputra!

It is because some man or woman is not a donor and does not practice giving toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or the poor and lowly who come as beggars—by not providing them with food, drink, clothing, garlands, ointments, beds, dwellings, lamps, or attendants. Because of this conduct, because of this condition, and on account of this conduct, when their body breaks up at death, they are reborn in an evil destination, in hell; and having been born here in the human world, they possess little wealth.
Why is that? Māluṅkyaputta, because he practiced the conduct of amassing small amounts of wealth, it causes some man or woman to possess little wealth.
This, Māluṅkyaputta!
One should know this as the result of such conduct.
Furthermore, Māluṅkyāputra, what is the cause and what is the condition by which a certain man or woman comes to possess great wealth?
"O Māluṅkyaputta!

Suppose there is a certain man or woman who acts as a donor, giving to recluses and brahmins, to the poor, the lowly, and those who come as beggars—giving food and drink, clothing and bedding, garlands and ointments, dwellings and lamps, and attendants. Because of this conduct, conditioned by this conduct, and on account of this conduct, when the body breaks up at death, they are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world; and having been reborn here in the human world, they possess great wealth."
Why is that? Māluṅkyāputra!
Because he practiced the conduct of amassing great wealth, he causes certain men or women to possess much wealth.
This, Māluṅkyāputta,
you should know as the result of such conduct.
This, Māluṅkyāputta!
Furthermore, what is the cause and what is the condition that leads some men or women to possess evil wisdom? Māluṅkyaputta!

It is because some men or women, regarding sentient beings, do not go to inquire; that is to say, there are certain renowned śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, yet having gone to them, they do not inquire about the meaning at the appropriate time, nor do they discuss with those worthy ones: "What is wholesome and what is unwholesome?"
What is good and what is not good?
What is evil and what is ugly?
What is black and what is white?
What is the retribution of black and white?
What is the meaning of the Dharma seen in this life?
What is the meaning of the precepts for future lives?
"What is that which is wholesome and not unwholesome?
Having heard this from him, one does not train in accordance with reality.

Because of this conduct, conditioned by this conduct, and on account of this conduct, at the breaking up of the body after death, one is reborn in an evil destination, in hell; and when reborn here in the human world, one possesses unwholesome wisdom."
Why is this? Māluṅkyāputra!
Because that person has practiced unwholesome wisdom, it causes certain men or women to be unable to go and question him regarding the welfare of sentient beings.
This, Māluṅkyāputta,
you should know as the result of such conduct.
This, Māluṅkyāputta!
Furthermore, what is the cause and what is the condition by which some man or woman possesses wisdom?
Māluṅkyāputta!

It is because some man or woman goes to question those beings—namely, those renowned śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—and having approached them, asks about their meaning at the appropriate time, being able to discuss with them: "O worthy ones, what is wholesome and what is unwholesome?"
What is good and what is not good?
What is ugly and what is sublime?
What is black and what is white?
What is the retribution of black and white?
What is the meaning of the Dharma as seen in this life?
What is the meaning of the precepts regarding future lives?
"What is that which is wholesome and not unwholesome?
Having heard it from him, one should learn it accordingly.

By means of this practice and conditioned by this practice, because of this practice, at the breaking up of the body after death, one is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly realm; and when reborn here in the human world, one possesses wisdom."
Why is this so? Māluṅkyāputra!
Because he has practiced with wisdom, he enables certain men or women to go and inquire on behalf of sentient beings.
This is it, Māluṅkyāputra!
You should know this because of the retribution for such conduct.
This, Māluṅkyāputra!
If one performs actions that lead to a short life, having performed them, one will experience a short life;
if one performs actions that lead to a long life, having performed them, one will experience a long life.
If one performs actions that lead to illness, having performed them, one will have much sickness.
If one performs unwholesome actions, having performed them, one will have no illness;
if one performs ugly actions, having performed them, one will receive ugliness;
if one performs actions of beautiful form and appearance, having performed them, one will receive a beautiful form and appearance.
If one performs actions that have limited capacity, having performed them, one will experience results of limited capacity;
if one performs actions that have great capacity, having performed them, one will experience results of great capacity.
If one performs base and lowly actions, having performed them, one will receive a base and lowly rebirth;
if one performs noble and honorable actions, having performed them, one will receive a noble and honorable rebirth.
If one performs actions involving meager wealth, having performed them, one will receive meager wealth.
If one performs actions involving abundant wealth, having performed them, one will receive abundant wealth.
If one performs actions involving corrupt wisdom, having performed them, one will receive corrupt wisdom;
if one performs actions involving true wisdom, having performed them, one will receive true wisdom.
This, Māluṅkyāputta,
is what I have previously taught.
This, Māluṅkyāputta!

According to the actions performed by sentient beings—whether through causal action or conditional action—it is because of these actions that sentient beings, in their various circumstances, experience degrees of high and low, or good and evil.
"It is finished, Gautama! It is finished, Gautama!
Yes, Blessed One!"
I now take refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus.
O World-Honored One!
From this day forth for as long as life lasts, I shall maintain the status of an upāsaka and abstain from taking life; I now take refuge.
"Indeed, Blessed One!

From this day forward, just as when entering the homes of other upāsakas in Śrāvastī, so too shall it be when entering the home of Tora; may we cause the house of Tora to be benefited by righteousness and attain peace for a long night."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the World-Honored One had said, Śuka Māṭhara the Tauriya rejoiced and withdrew.
This concludes the *Śukopama Sūtra* (The Parrot Sūtra) as spoken by the Buddha.
